latin: aiunt quidam et Genesim in Hebraico ita incipere, In principio deus fecit sibi� filium. hoc ut firmum non sit alia me argumenta deducunt ab ipsa dei dispositione qua fuit ante mundi constitutionem ad usque filii generationem.
latin_edition: Latin Library transcription (section numbers [n] as printed on that page; the page names no edition, not collated against Kroymann CSEL 47 or Oehler). Read via raw download. Garbled character (U+FFFD) inside 'sibi' and 'filium' gap in the source transcription, reproduced as printed. [FLAG: source contains garbled character]
english: There are some who allege that even Genesis opens thus in Hebrew: In the beginning God made for Himself a Son. As there is no ground for this, I am led to other arguments derived from God's own dispensation, in which He existed before the creation of the world, up to the generation of the Son.
translator: Peter Holmes, ANF vol. 3 (ed. Roberts, Donaldson, Coxe); text as on newadvent.org (rev. Kevin Knight)
edition: Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 3, Buffalo: Christian Literature Pub. Co., 1887 printing (archive.org/details/antenicenefather03buff, public domain; NA gives original 1885)
what_it_says: Opponents claim Genesis opens in Hebrew as God making himself a Son; Tertullian rejects that reading and argues from God's dispensation before creation.
use: objection (the Genesis reading cited against an eternal Son), answered by appeal to the pre-creation dispensation
limits: Tertullian reports the opponents' reading without an argued Hebrew analysis; the Latin Library text has a garbled character after 'sibi' (flagged).

latin: ante omnia enim deus erat solus, ipse sibi et mundus et locus et omnia. solus autem quia nihil aliud extrinsecus praeter illum. ceterum ne tunc quidem solus: habebat enim secum quam habebat in semetipso rationem, suam scilicet. rationalis enim deus, et ratio in ipso prius, et ita ab ipso omnia: quae ratio sensus ipsius est.
latin_edition: Latin Library transcription (section numbers [n] as printed on that page; the page names no edition, not collated against Kroymann CSEL 47 or Oehler). Read via raw download.
english: For before all things God was alone — being in Himself and for Himself universe, and space, and all things. Moreover, He was alone, because there was nothing external to Him but Himself. Yet even not then was He alone; for He had with Him that which He possessed in Himself, that is to say, His own Reason. For God is rational, and Reason was first in Him; and so all things were from Himself.
translator: Peter Holmes, ANF vol. 3 (ed. Roberts, Donaldson, Coxe); text as on newadvent.org (rev. Kevin Knight)
edition: Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 3, Buffalo: Christian Literature Pub. Co., 1887 printing (archive.org/details/antenicenefather03buff, public domain; NA gives original 1885)
what_it_says: Before creation God was not alone, because His own Reason (ratio) was in Him from the beginning, and all things came from that Reason.
use: supports Trinitarian reading (a Reason-Word in God before creation, not a later addition)
limits: 'Ratio' here is the divine intelligence; Arian and Socinian readers take 'ratio' as an attribute, which Tertullian himself flags in ch. 7 ('liable to be deemed a mere attribute').

latin: tamen et sic nihil interest. nam etsi deus nondum sermonem suum miserat, proinde eum cum ipsa et in ipsa ratione intra semetipsum habebat, tacite cogitando et disponendo secum quae per sermonem mox erat dicturus: cum ratione enim sua cogitans atque disponens, sermonem eam efficiebat quam sermone tractabat.
latin_edition: Latin Library transcription (section numbers [n] as printed on that page; the page names no edition, not collated against Kroymann CSEL 47 or Oehler). Read via raw download.
english: Not that this distinction is of any practical moment. For although God had not yet sent out His Word, He still had Him within Himself, both in company with and included within His very Reason, as He silently planned and arranged within Himself everything which He was afterwards about to utter through His Word. Now, while He was thus planning and arranging with His own Reason, He was actually causing that to become Word which He was dealing with in the way of Word or Discourse.
translator: Peter Holmes, ANF vol. 3 (ed. Roberts, Donaldson, Coxe); text as on newadvent.org (rev. Kevin Knight)
edition: Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 3, Buffalo: Christian Literature Pub. Co., 1887 printing (archive.org/details/antenicenefather03buff, public domain; NA gives original 1885)
what_it_says: Although God had not yet sent out His Word, He had it within Himself in Reason, planning what He would later utter through the Word.
use: explanation of hard passage: 'Word within God' before the 'sending' (prolatio) is a pre-creation distinction within God
limits: Tertullian's analogy is human thought; 'sermo' inside 'ratio' can be read as a mental process only (modalist or attribute reading).

latin: quodcunque cogitaveris sermo est, quodcunque senseris ratio est: loquaris illud in animo necesse est, et dum loqueris conlocutorem pateris sermonem, in quo inest haec ipsa ratio qua cum eo cogitans loquaris per quem loquens cogitas. ita secundus quodammodo in te est sermo per quem loqueris cogitando et per quem cogitas loquendo: ipse sermo alius est.
latin_edition: Latin Library transcription (section numbers [n] as printed on that page; the page names no edition, not collated against Kroymann CSEL 47 or Oehler). Read via raw download.
english: Thus, in a certain sense, the word is a second person within you, through which in thinking you utter speech, and through which also, (by reciprocity of process,) in uttering speech you generate thought. The word is itself a different thing from yourself.
translator: Peter Holmes, ANF vol. 3 (ed. Roberts, Donaldson, Coxe); text as on newadvent.org (rev. Kevin Knight)
edition: Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 3, Buffalo: Christian Literature Pub. Co., 1887 printing (archive.org/details/antenicenefather03buff, public domain; NA gives original 1885)
what_it_says: Human thought shows a word that is 'a second person' within the thinker yet distinct from him; Tertullian applies this analogy to God's Word.
use: answer to objection (the Word as a mere attribute): the Word is 'another thing' (alius) within the Speaker
limits: Analogy only; Tertullian's word 'secundus' (second) is the point Arian readers press as subordination.

latin: quanto ergo plenius hoc agitur in deo cuius tu quoque imago et similitudo censeris, quod habeat in se etiam tacendo rationem et in ratione sermonem? possum itaque non temere praestruxisse et tunc deum ante universitatis constitutionem solum non fuisse, habentem in semetipso proinde rationem et in ratione sermonem quem secundum a se faceret agitando intra se.
latin_edition: Latin Library transcription (section numbers [n] as printed on that page; the page names no edition, not collated against Kroymann CSEL 47 or Oehler). Read via raw download.
english: I may therefore without rashness first lay this down (as a fixed principle) that even then before the creation of the universe God was not alone, since He had within Himself both Reason, and, inherent in Reason, His Word, which He made second to Himself by agitating it within Himself.
translator: Peter Holmes, ANF vol. 3 (ed. Roberts, Donaldson, Coxe); text as on newadvent.org (rev. Kevin Knight)
edition: Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 3, Buffalo: Christian Literature Pub. Co., 1887 printing (archive.org/details/antenicenefather03buff, public domain; NA gives original 1885)
what_it_says: Before the universe, God was not alone: He had Reason and, in Reason, His Word, which He made 'second to Himself' by 'agitating' it within Himself.
use: supports Trinitarian reading (the Word present with God before creation)
limits: 'Faceret' and 'agitando' (make, stir) are the verbs anti-Trinitarians use for creation; 'secundum a se' reads as 'made second'.

latin: quid enim sapientius ratione dei sive sermone? itaque sophiam quoque exaudi, ut secundam personam conditam: primo, Dominus creavit me initium viarum in opera sua, priusquam terram faceret, priusquam montes collocarentur; ante omnes autem colles generavit me— in sensu suo scilicet condens et generans.
latin_edition: Latin Library transcription (section numbers [n] as printed on that page; the page names no edition, not collated against Kroymann CSEL 47 or Oehler). Read via raw download.
english: This power and disposition of the Divine Intelligence is set forth also in the Scriptures under the name of Σοφία, Wisdom; for what can be better entitled to the name of Wisdom than the Reason or the Word of God? Listen therefore to Wisdom herself, constituted in the character of a Second Person: At the first the Lord created me as the beginning of His ways, with a view to His own works, before He made the earth, before the mountains were settled; moreover, before all the hills did He beget me; Proverbs 8:22-25 that is to say, He created and generated me in His own intelligence.
translator: Peter Holmes, ANF vol. 3 (ed. Roberts, Donaldson, Coxe); text as on newadvent.org (rev. Kevin Knight)
edition: Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 3, Buffalo: Christian Literature Pub. Co., 1887 printing (archive.org/details/antenicenefather03buff, public domain; NA gives original 1885)
what_it_says: Wisdom (Prov. 8) is the Word's own intelligence; Scripture presents Wisdom as a 'second person' that God created and generated 'in His own intelligence'.
use: explanation of hard passage: 'created' (condidit/creavit) is read as conception in the divine mind before the Word's generation
limits: Tertullian uses 'conditam' (created) of the Second Person; Arian readers take Prov. 8:22 'created' literally. Not checked against Athanasius or other Nicene exegesis of Prov. 8:22 in this pass.

latin: dehinc adsistentem eam ipsa separatione cognosce: Cum pararet, inquit, caelum aderam illi simul; et quomodo fortia faciebat super ventos quae sursum nubila, et quomodo tutos ponebat fontes eius quae sub caelo, ego eram cum illo compingens, ego eram ad quam gaudebat; cottidie autem oblectabar in persona ipsius.
latin_edition: Latin Library transcription (section numbers [n] as printed on that page; the page names no edition, not collated against Kroymann CSEL 47 or Oehler). Read via raw download. Latin Library has 'cottidie'; Migne PL 2 has 'quotidie' and 'et cum fortia faciebat' (Migne variants; ANF follows the Migne/Holmes text).
english: Then, again, observe the distinction between them implied in the companionship of Wisdom with the Lord. When He prepared the heaven, says Wisdom, I was present with Him; and when He made His strong places upon the winds, which are the clouds above; and when He secured the fountains, (and all things) which are beneath the sky, I was by, arranging all things with Him; I was by, in whom He delighted; and daily, too, did I rejoice in His presence.
translator: Peter Holmes, ANF vol. 3 (ed. Roberts, Donaldson, Coxe); text as on newadvent.org (rev. Kevin Knight)
edition: Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 3, Buffalo: Christian Literature Pub. Co., 1887 printing (archive.org/details/antenicenefather03buff, public domain; NA gives original 1885)
what_it_says: Wisdom says that she was present with God at creation and rejoiced in His presence: a distinction of persons (Wisdom 'beside' God) before the world.
use: supports distinction of persons (companionship, 'cum illo', 'ad quam gaudebat')
limits: Arian readers take this companion Wisdom as a created instrument; Tertullian's reading relies on 'Wisdom = the Word'.

latin: nam ut primum deus voluit ea quae cum sophia et ratione et sermone disposuerat intra se in substantias et species suas edere, ipsum primum protulit sermonem habentem in se individuas suas rationem et sophiam, ut per ipsum fierent universa per quem erant cogitata atque disposita, immo et facta iam quantum in dei sensu:
latin_edition: Latin Library transcription (section numbers [n] as printed on that page; the page names no edition, not collated against Kroymann CSEL 47 or Oehler). Read via raw download. Migne PL 2 reads 'ipsum primum protulit sermonem, habentem in se individuas suas, Rationem et Sophiam'; Latin Library has 'habentem in se individuas suas rationem et sophiam' and 'cum sophia et ratione et sermone' (Migne: 'cum sophiae ratione et sermone').
english: Now, as soon as it pleased God to put forth into their respective substances and forms the things which He had planned and ordered within Himself, in conjunction with His Wisdom's Reason and Word, He first put forth the Word Himself, having within Him His own inseparable Reason and Wisdom, in order that all things might be made through Him through whom they had been planned and disposed, yea, and already made, so far forth as (they were) in the mind and intelligence of God.
translator: Peter Holmes, ANF vol. 3 (ed. Roberts, Donaldson, Coxe); text as on newadvent.org (rev. Kevin Knight)
edition: Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 3, Buffalo: Christian Literature Pub. Co., 1887 printing (archive.org/details/antenicenefather03buff, public domain; NA gives original 1885)
what_it_says: When God chose to bring His planned things into substance, He first 'put forth' (protulit) the Word, having within Him His inseparable Reason and Wisdom, so that all things could be made through Him.
use: supports Trinitarian reading (the Word is the first 'prolation', with Reason and Wisdom inseparable in Him, before creation)
limits: 'Protulit' (brought forth) is the verb Arians cite for the Word's coming-to-be; the same chapter calls it 'nativitas' (see next item). Tertullian's Latin 'prolatio' is contrasted with Valentinian emanation in ch. 8.

latin: Tunc igitur etiam ipse sermo speciem et ornatum suum sumit, sonum et vocem, cum dicit deus, Fiat lux. haec est nativitas perfecta sermonis, dum ex deo procedit;
latin_edition: Latin Library transcription (section numbers [n] as printed on that page; the page names no edition, not collated against Kroymann CSEL 47 or Oehler). Read via raw download. Migne PL 2 reads the same 'Tunc igitur etiam ipse sermo speciem et ornatum suum sumit'; I searched the exact phrase on the web and found no hit, but read it in two Latin texts.
english: Then, therefore, does the Word also Himself assume His own form and glorious garb, His own sound and vocal utterance, when God says, Let there be light. Genesis 1:3 This is the perfect nativity of the Word, when He proceeds forth from God
translator: Peter Holmes, ANF vol. 3 (ed. Roberts, Donaldson, Coxe); text as on newadvent.org (rev. Kevin Knight)
edition: Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 3, Buffalo: Christian Literature Pub. Co., 1887 printing (archive.org/details/antenicenefather03buff, public domain; NA gives original 1885)
what_it_says: At God's word 'Let there be light' the Word takes on form and voice; this is the 'perfect nativity' of the Word as He proceeds from God.
use: explanation of hard passage: the 'then' is the manifestation of the Word in creation, after His prior conception (ch. 6)
limits: The text dates the 'perfect nativity' to the moment of creation ('tunc ... cum dicit deus'); this is the core of the anti-Trinitarian objection. I did not read the secondary literature on this point in this pass.

latin: exinde eum patrem sibi faciens de quo procedendo filius factus est primogenitus, ut ante omnia genitus, et unigenitus, ut solus ex deo genitus, proprie de vulva cordis ipsius secundum quod et pater ipse testatur, Eructavit cor meum sermonem optimum;
latin_edition: Latin Library transcription (section numbers [n] as printed on that page; the page names no edition, not collated against Kroymann CSEL 47 or Oehler). Read via raw download. Latin Library: 'eum patrem sibi faciens'. Migne PL 2 (earlychurchtexts cross-check): 'eum parem sibi faciens'.
english: Thus does He make Him equal to Him: for by proceeding from Himself He became His first-begotten Son, because begotten before all things; Colossians 1:15 and His only-begotten also, because alone begotten of God, in a way peculiar to Himself, from the womb of His own heart — even as the Father Himself testifies: My heart, says He, has emitted my most excellent Word.
translator: Peter Holmes, ANF vol. 3 (ed. Roberts, Donaldson, Coxe); text as on newadvent.org (rev. Kevin Knight)
edition: Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 3, Buffalo: Christian Literature Pub. Co., 1887 printing (archive.org/details/antenicenefather03buff, public domain; NA gives original 1885)
what_it_says: The Word is made 'equal' to God, is the first-born before all things and only-begotten from the heart of God; the Father's own words (Ps. 44) testify to this.
use: supports divinity of the Son (begotten 'before all things', 'from the heart'); also shows the Son is 'of God' not made from nothing
limits: TEXT-CRITICAL FLAG: Latin Library reads 'patrem sibi faciens' ('making him Father to himself'); Migne PL 2 reads 'parem sibi faciens' ('making him equal to himself'), which matches the ANF 'equal to Him'. Use the Migne reading only with that note.

latin: quid est enim, dices, sermo nisi vox et sonus oris, et sicut grammatici tradunt aer offensus intellegibilis auditu, ceterum vacuum nescio quid et inane et incorporale? at ego nihil dico de deo inane et vacuum prodire potuisse, ut non de inani et vacuo prolatum, nec carere substantia quod de tanta substantia processit et tantas substantias fecit;
latin_edition: Latin Library transcription (section numbers [n] as printed on that page; the page names no edition, not collated against Kroymann CSEL 47 or Oehler). Read via raw download.
english: For you will say, what is a word, but a voice and sound of the mouth, and (as the grammarians teach) air when struck against, intelligible to the ear, but for the rest a sort of void, empty, and incorporeal thing. I, on the contrary, contend that nothing empty and void could have come forth from God, seeing that it is not put forth from that which is empty and void; nor could that possibly be devoid of substance which has proceeded from so great a substance, and has produced such mighty substances:
translator: Peter Holmes, ANF vol. 3 (ed. Roberts, Donaldson, Coxe); text as on newadvent.org (rev. Kevin Knight)
edition: Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 3, Buffalo: Christian Literature Pub. Co., 1887 printing (archive.org/details/antenicenefather03buff, public domain; NA gives original 1885)
what_it_says: Opponents say a 'word' is only breath and sound, a void; Tertullian replies that nothing empty could come from God and that the Word, from so great a substance, has substance.
use: answer to objection (the Word as mere voice or attribute), by appeal to 'substantia' and to the Word as a real person
limits: Tertullian's 'substantia' is material and corporeal (see the next item); the Nicene term ousia is not the same concept.

latin: in qua effigie dei? utique in aliqua, non tamen in nulla: quis enim negabit deum corpus esse, etsi deus spiritus est? spiritus enim corpus sui generis in sua effigie.
latin_edition: Latin Library transcription (section numbers [n] as printed on that page; the page names no edition, not collated against Kroymann CSEL 47 or Oehler). Read via raw download.
english: In what form of God? Of course he means in some form, not in none. For who will deny that God is a body, although God is a Spirit? John 4:24 For Spirit has a bodily substance of its own kind, in its own form.
translator: Peter Holmes, ANF vol. 3 (ed. Roberts, Donaldson, Coxe); text as on newadvent.org (rev. Kevin Knight)
edition: Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 3, Buffalo: Christian Literature Pub. Co., 1887 printing (archive.org/details/antenicenefather03buff, public domain; NA gives original 1885)
what_it_says: Tertullian says the Word is in 'some' form of God and that God is a body although God is Spirit, because Spirit has a bodily substance of its own kind.
use: objection (corporeal God): Tertullian's own words; no full answer in Nicene terms is given here
limits: Opponents' best-known quotation against Tertullian's orthodoxy. The defence (Stoic/material sense of 'corpus' for Spirit) is not verified in this pass.

latin: quaecunque ergo substantia sermonis fuit, illam dico personam et illi nomen filii vindico, et dam filium agnosco secundum a patre defendo.
latin_edition: Latin Library transcription (section numbers [n] as printed on that page; the page names no edition, not collated against Kroymann CSEL 47 or Oehler). Read via raw download. Latin Library prints 'et dam filium agnosco'; Migne PL 2 'et dum filium agnosco' (variant).
english: Whatever, therefore, was the substance of the Word that I designate a Person, I claim for it the name of Son; and while I recognize the Son, I assert His distinction as second to the Father.
translator: Peter Holmes, ANF vol. 3 (ed. Roberts, Donaldson, Coxe); text as on newadvent.org (rev. Kevin Knight)
edition: Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 3, Buffalo: Christian Literature Pub. Co., 1887 printing (archive.org/details/antenicenefather03buff, public domain; NA gives original 1885)
what_it_says: Whatever the substance of the Word, Tertullian calls it a person, claims the name Son for it, and defends its distinction as 'second' to the Father.
use: supports distinction of persons (persona + Son) and the claim that the Word is a person, not an attribute
limits: 'Secundum a patre' is read by Arian and subordinationist critics as 'subordinate'; 'substantia' is material (see 7.8). The Latin Library prints 'dam filium' (Migne has 'dum').

latin: Hoc si qui putaverit me probolh_n aliquam introducere, id est prolationem rei alterius ex altera, quod facit Valentinus alium atque alium aeonem de aeone producens, primo quidem dicam tibi, non ideo non utitur et veritas vocabulo isto et re ac censu eius quia et haeresis utatur: immo haeresis potius ex veritate accepit quod ad mendacium suum strueret.
latin_edition: Latin Library transcription (section numbers [n] as printed on that page; the page names no edition, not collated against Kroymann CSEL 47 or Oehler). Read via raw download. Greek term transliterated by the Latin Library as 'probolh_n'.
english: If any man from this shall think that I am introducing some προβολή — that is to say, some prolation of one thing out of another, as Valentinus does when he sets forth Æon from Æon, one after another — then this is my first reply to you: Truth must not therefore refrain from the use of such a term, and its reality and meaning, because heresy also employs it. The fact is, heresy has rather taken it from Truth, in order to mould it into its own counterfeit.
translator: Peter Holmes, ANF vol. 3 (ed. Roberts, Donaldson, Coxe); text as on newadvent.org (rev. Kevin Knight)
edition: Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 3, Buffalo: Christian Literature Pub. Co., 1887 printing (archive.org/details/antenicenefather03buff, public domain; NA gives original 1885)
what_it_says: If someone thinks Tertullian introduces the Valentinian 'prolation', he replies that truth may use the term that heresy uses, since heresy took it from truth.
use: answer to objection (Valentinian emanation): 'prolatio' is a term the truth uses; the difference is in the sense
limits: The Greek term (probolh) is Valentinian; Tertullian concedes the word is shared; the Latin Library transliterates the Greek as 'probolh_n'.

latin: sermo ergo et in patre semper, sicut dicit, Ego in patre: et apud deum semper, sicut scriptum est, Et sermo erat apud deum: et nunquam separatus a patre aut alias a patre quia Ego et pater unum sumus.
latin_edition: Latin Library transcription (section numbers [n] as printed on that page; the page names no edition, not collated against Kroymann CSEL 47 or Oehler). Read via raw download.
english: The Word, therefore, is both always in the Father, as He says, I am in the Father; John 14:11 and is always with God, according to what is written, And the Word was with God; John 1:1 and never separate from the Father, or other than the Father, since I and the Father are one.
translator: Peter Holmes, ANF vol. 3 (ed. Roberts, Donaldson, Coxe); text as on newadvent.org (rev. Kevin Knight)
edition: Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 3, Buffalo: Christian Literature Pub. Co., 1887 printing (archive.org/details/antenicenefather03buff, public domain; NA gives original 1885)
what_it_says: The Word is always in the Father and with God and never separate from the Father, citing John 14:11, 1:1 and 10:30.
use: supports unity of substance (Word never separated; 'unum' from John 10:30)
limits: Arian and Socinian readers take John 10:30 'one' as moral unity, not unity of substance; Tertullian's argument here is by quotation.

latin: haec erit probolh_ veritatis, custos unitatis, qua prolatum dicimus filium a patre sed non separatum. protulit enim deus sermonem, quemadmodum etiam paracletus docet, sicut radix fruticem et fons fluvium et sol radium:
latin_edition: Latin Library transcription (section numbers [n] as printed on that page; the page names no edition, not collated against Kroymann CSEL 47 or Oehler). Read via raw download. Latin Library has the Greek 'probolh_' transliteration.
english: This will be the prolation, taught by the truth, the guardian of the Unity, wherein we declare that the Son is a prolation from the Father, without being separated from Him. For God sent forth the Word, as the Paraclete also declares, just as the root puts forth the tree, and the fountain the river, and the sun the ray.
translator: Peter Holmes, ANF vol. 3 (ed. Roberts, Donaldson, Coxe); text as on newadvent.org (rev. Kevin Knight)
edition: Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 3, Buffalo: Christian Literature Pub. Co., 1887 printing (archive.org/details/antenicenefather03buff, public domain; NA gives original 1885)
what_it_says: The Son is a 'prolation' from the Father without separation, as the Paraclete teaches: God sent forth the Word as the root puts forth the tree, the fountain the river, the sun the ray.
use: supports Trinitarian reading (the Son proceeds from the Father, not separated); Holy Spirit appears in the same passage as Paraclete
limits: The analogies show derivation (the tree comes from the root, the ray from the sun), which anti-Trinitarians read as the Son being derived and so less than the Father. 'Protulit' and 'misit' (sent) are the verbs at issue.

latin: igitur secundum horum exemplorum formam profiteor me duos licere deum et sermonem� eius, patrem et filium ipsius: nam et radix et frutex duae res sunt sed coniunctae, et fons et flumen duae species sunt sed indivisae, et sol et radius duce formae sunt sed cohaerentes.
latin_edition: Latin Library transcription (section numbers [n] as printed on that page; the page names no edition, not collated against Kroymann CSEL 47 or Oehler). Read via raw download. Latin Library prints 'duce formae' (sic). [FLAG: source contains garbled character]
english: Following, therefore, the form of these analogies, I confess that I call God and His Word — the Father and His Son — two. For the root and the tree are distinctly two things, but correlatively joined; the fountain and the river are also two forms, but indivisible; so likewise the sun and the ray are two forms, but coherent ones.
translator: Peter Holmes, ANF vol. 3 (ed. Roberts, Donaldson, Coxe); text as on newadvent.org (rev. Kevin Knight)
edition: Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 3, Buffalo: Christian Literature Pub. Co., 1887 printing (archive.org/details/antenicenefather03buff, public domain; NA gives original 1885)
what_it_says: Tertullian confesses that God and His Word are 'two' by the form of the analogies: the root and tree, fountain and river, sun and ray are two forms joined without division.
use: answer to objection ('two' = two Gods, the Praxean charge), by the analogy of 'two forms' in one substance
limits: 'Two forms' (formae) and 'two things' (res) are not the Nicene language of hypostasis; the Latin Library prints 'duce formae' (sic; sense 'duae formae').

latin: secundus autem ubi est, duo sunt, et tertius ubi est, tres sunt. tertius enim est spiritus� a deo et filio, sicut tertius a radice fructus ex frutice et tertius a fonte rivus ex flamine et tertius a sole apex ex radio: nihil tamen a matrice alienatur a qua proprietates suas ducit. ita trinitas per consertos et connexos gradus a patre decurrens et monarchiae nihil obstrepit et oeconomiae statum protegit.
latin_edition: Latin Library transcription (section numbers [n] as printed on that page; the page names no edition, not collated against Kroymann CSEL 47 or Oehler). Read via raw download. [FLAG: source contains garbled character]
english: Where, however, there is a second, there must be two; and where there is a third, there must be three. Now the Spirit indeed is third from God and the Son; just as the fruit of the tree is third from the root, or as the stream out of the river is third from the fountain, or as the apex of the ray is third from the sun. Nothing, however, is alien from that original source whence it derives its own properties. In like manner the Trinity, flowing down from the Father through intertwined and connected steps, does not at all disturb the Monarchy, while it at the same time guards the state of the Economy.
translator: Peter Holmes, ANF vol. 3 (ed. Roberts, Donaldson, Coxe); text as on newadvent.org (rev. Kevin Knight)
edition: Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 3, Buffalo: Christian Literature Pub. Co., 1887 printing (archive.org/details/antenicenefather03buff, public domain; NA gives original 1885)
what_it_says: A second is two and a third is three: the Spirit is third from God and the Son as fruit is third from the root, and the Trinity flowing from the Father does not disturb the Monarchy.
use: supports Holy Spirit as third person, and 'trinitas' as a term of the economy; answers the charge that the Trinity destroys the Monarchy
limits: 'Tertius' gives order (gradus), not identity; 'economia' is the phrase opponents read as subordination; the text does not state the Spirit's divinity in these words.
